text.hook:
"deque is just a vector that can also grow at the front."
That answer fails C++ interviews.

Five containers, their real memory layouts, plus 6 myths. Swipe ➜ and save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Four memory layouts
2. deque by the numbers
3. list, forward_list, array
4. Adaptors and pop() returning void
5. Which container for which need
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: deque, list, forward_list, array and the adaptors: what each one costs and why.

slides.title: The layout decides everything

cards.label: Contiguous
cards.text: `vector`, `string`: one contiguous buffer. `std::array` inside the object.

cards.label: Blocks + map
cards.text: `deque`: fixed-size blocks and an array of block pointers.

slides.takeaway: Default to `vector`. Pick another one for a concrete reason: front growth, stable addresses, splicing, fixed size.

slides.title: Random access without contiguity
rows: fixed blocks: index math is division and modulo
80 bytes plus two allocations: map and one block
slides.takeaway: End insertion never moves elements: references survive, iterators do not.

cards.label: std::list
cards.text: O(1) insert and erase **at an iterator you hold**. `splice` relinks nodes. Member `sort`, `merge`, `unique`.

cards.label: std::forward_list
cards.text: One pointer (8 bytes, libstdc++). No `size()`. Works *after* a position: `insert_after`, `before_begin()`.

cards.label: std::array
cards.text: Aggregate around `T[N]`: no heap, copyable, comparable, `constexpr`. `swap` is O(N).

slides.title: Wrappers, not containers
rows: `vector` as a binary heap: O(log n) push and pop
slides.takeaway: `pop()` returns `void` because returning by value could throw after removal and lose the element. Read `top()` first.

slides.title: Need, then container
rows: Push and pop at both ends, indexing
slides.takeaway: Stable addresses with indexing: `deque` grown only at the ends, or `vector<unique_ptr<T>>`.

slides.hero:
A vector shift
usually beats
a list relink.
slides.lead: For small and medium N, a sequential `memmove` beats a chain of cache misses. Choose `list` for semantics, not speed. Measure.

items.myth: "deque is a vector that can also grow at the front."
items.truth: It is a block map: not contiguous, no `data()`, no `reserve()`, bigger fixed cost.
Fixed per element type (libstdc++: 512 bytes). That is what makes indexing O(1).
References never move on end insertion. Only iterators are invalidated.

items.myth: "list insertion is O(1), so list beats vector for inserts."
items.truth: Only with an iterator in hand. Finding the position is O(n) and dominates.

slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
A list of 3 numbers. std::sort, the algorithm everyone knows.
What could go wrong?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Same code with a vector works. The list changes one thing.

slides.title:
Sort a list.
What happens?

bullets: `std::sort` needs **random access** iterators: it computes `last - first` and jumps to midpoints.
`list` iterators are bidirectional: no `-`, no `+ n`.
The error appears deep inside `std::sort`. C++20 `std::ranges::sort(l)` names the unmet `random_access_range` constraint instead.

slides.title: Use the member sort
slides.tip: `l.sort()` is a stable merge sort, O(n log n). It relinks nodes, so every iterator stays valid.
slides.takeaway: The iterator category decides which algorithms you can call.

text.hook:
Two priority queues. One uses the default, one uses std::greater.
"greater" means biggest first. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Same four values pushed into both queues.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: The default is a max-heap. `std::greater` gives a min-heap
bullets: The comparator means "has lower priority than", not "comes first".
With `std::less` (default), the largest value has the highest priority: max-heap.
With `std::greater`, a larger value counts as **lower** priority, so the smallest comes out first.

slides.title: Earliest event first
slides.tip: `priority_queue` is not stable: without `seq`, equal times come out in unspecified order.
slides.takeaway: "Earliest first" needs `a.time > b.time`, the opposite of what the name suggests.

text.hook:
list::unique(). The name says it all:
every value appears once afterwards. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Seven values, three distinct. Count what is left.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: `unique()` collapses runs of **consecutive** equal elements, like `std::unique`.
The runs `2 2` and `3 3` collapse. The separate 1s and 2s stay.
Since C++20, `unique()` returns the number removed: 2 here.
slides.wrong: "1 2 3: unique keeps one of each value"

slides.title: Sort first, then unique
slides.takeaway: unique means "collapse adjacent equal elements", not "make the values unique".

text.hook:
std::array is the safe, modern C array.
So std::array<int, 3> a; starts zeroed. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.

slides.title: Which statement is true?

slides.verdict_sub: Line 1 is guaranteed. Reading `a[0]` reads an indeterminate value
bullets: `std::array` is an aggregate. `a` is default-initialized: for `int`, no initialization at all.
`c{7}` sets the first element and value-initializes the rest: `7 0 0`.
Our GCC 11 runs printed a different garbage number each time.

slides.title: Write the braces
bullets: GCC 11 warns (`-Wuninitialized`) only with `-O2`, not at `-O0`.
`std::array<std::string, 3> s;` is fine: class types are default-constructed.
slides.takeaway: `std::array` follows C array initialization rules. `{}` gives zeros.
